title: When something goes wrong
job: Problems, asking for help, complaining calmly
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: ʿafwan + , + hunāka mushkila fī + al- + N

rules.text: "ʿindī means I have" is memorable and leaves you unable to explain ʿindahā, or the past kāna ʿindī, or why there is no verb to conjugate. The law: ʿind- is a PREPOSITION meaning "at", and Arabic expresses having by locating a thing at a person.
Negating a verb is lā, exactly as M3 of the level below taught: hādhā lā yaʿmal. laysa, which M7 opened, is for a sentence with no verb, and this module names it and does not use it.
aḥtāj takes ilā before what is needed: aḥtāj ilā musāʿada. A bare object after it is the English shape and it is wrong.
An imperative can carry its object: sāʿidnī is "help me" in one word, built like M1's aʿṭinī. The -nī is the same "me" in both.
Arabic complains through the frame, not through volume: ʿafwan, hunāka mushkila… An unframed statement of the fault is an accusation, and framing it costs two words.

sentences.cue: I have a problem at home

words.note: Feminine, and indefinite here because the problem is news. With al- it becomes the problem you were already discussing.

sentences.trap: ʿindī is not a verb, and this is the sentence to notice it in: there is nothing here that conjugates, and the past would be kāna ʿindī with kāna doing all the work.
sentences.sound: MUSH-ki-la, three short syllables with the stress at the front.

variations.cue: I have a problem with the car

M2's suffix, and an adjective after the noun

mistake.why: The suffix already says who. anā in front is the English shape and reads as insistence.

sentences.usage: Opening a complaint about a thing rather than a person, which is the polite order.
sentences.mnemonic: The problem is AT you, not owned by you.

words.note: Built on the same three letters as M4's al-ʿamal, "work", from the level below. Of a machine it means functions; of a person, is employed.

sentences.trap: lā, not laysa. There is a verb here, so the ordinary negative does the job — and M7's laysa is only for sentences without one.
sentences.sound: YAʿ-mal, with the ʿayn tightening the throat after the first vowel.

variations.changed: the thing named instead of pointed at
a feminine thing, so the verb takes ta-

mistake.why: laysa negates a sentence with no verb. Here there is one, so it is lā yaʿmal.

sentences.usage: Reporting a fault. On its own it is flat, and S05 shows how to soften it.
sentences.mnemonic: A verb takes lā; a sentence without one takes laysa.

words.note: An imperative with -nī glued on, built exactly like M1's aʿṭinī. The feminine adds -ī before the -nī: sāʿidīnī.

sentences.trap: One word for two English ones, and the object is inside it. Arabic never lets a pronoun stand loose after a verb.
sentences.sound: SĀ-ʿid-nī, with the ʿayn in the middle and the stress at the front.

variations.changed: the feminine, which the script shows
M1's other softener
M1's softest frame, which is what to use with a stranger

mistake.why: The pronoun is part of the word: sāʿidnī.

sentences.usage: Direct, and softened by min faḍlika. With someone you have not spoken to, the third variation is better.
sentences.mnemonic: The me is inside the verb.

words.note: Takes ilā before what is needed, which English does not lead you to expect. It is stronger than urīd: a want against a need.
The noun from the same three letters as sāʿidnī. Seeing the pair side by side is worth more than learning either alone.

sentences.trap: aḥtāj māʾ is not Arabic. The verb reaches its object through ilā, and dropping it is the English shape.
sentences.sound: aḥ-TĀJ, with the ḥ deep and the stress on the long ā.

mistake.why: aḥtāj takes ilā: aḥtāj ilā musāʿada.

sentences.usage: Stronger than urīd, and used when something has actually gone wrong.

words.note: One word for the whole thing, where English needs two. ṣ is emphatic and s is a sun letter, so al- would assimilate: aṣ-ṣudāʿ.

sentences.trap: The same ʿind- frame does a problem, a car and a headache. Arabic locates all three at the person, which is why one frame covers them.

sentences.usage: At a pharmacy, at a desk, to a friend. The same frame as every other complaint in the module.
sentences.mnemonic: One frame for every kind of trouble.

sentences.cue: I forgot the key at home

words.note: The perfect with -tu, "I", written in full as the course's romanization requires. The Arabic line is نسيت for nasītu and nasīta alike.

sentences.trap: Another place where the two lines carry different information: نسيت is I forgot, you forgot and she forgot. Only the romanization says which.
sentences.sound: na-SĪ-tu, with the stress on the long ī.

variations.cue: I forgot the letter at home
variations.changed: M7's risāla as the object
M7's two-noun possession as the object
the you-form, which the Arabic line spells identically

mistake.why: The person-suffix carries the person and is never dropped: nasītu for I.

sentences.usage: The commonest small disaster there is, and the past tense here is L1-M5's doing exactly its job.
sentences.mnemonic: The suffix is the person, and the script does not show it.

sentences.cue: The key got lost in the market

words.note: The thing does the losing, not the person: ḍāʿa al-miftāḥ. Arabic has no comfortable way to say "I lost it" that puts the blame on you.

sentences.trap: The verb comes FIRST and the key is its subject. That word order is ordinary in Arabic and impossible in English, and M10 makes a rule of it.
sentences.sound: ḌĀ-ʿa, with the ḍ emphatic and the ʿayn closing it.

variations.changed: a feminine subject, so the verb takes -at

variations.cue: The key got lost, I need help
variations.changed: the problem and the request together
asked, with hal in front and the verb still first

mistake.why: That is grammatical and puts the emphasis on the key rather than on what happened. Verb first is the neutral order, and M10 states the rule.

sentences.usage: Reporting a loss without accusing anybody, including yourself.
sentences.mnemonic: In Arabic the key loses itself.

sentences.cue: Excuse me, there's a problem with the bill

words.note: M7's row from the level below, announcing rather than pointing — the same second job M4 of this level gave it.

sentences.trap: Three softeners before the fault is named: ʿafwan, hunāka rather than a direct accusation, and mushkila rather than the thing that is wrong. That is how Arabic complains.
